extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in nonlinear time series analysis / dynamical systems (users of recurrence plots and RQA)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for computing and interpreting recurrence plots (RPs) and recurrence quantification analysis (RQA): choosing embedding/thresholds, selecting RQA measures (diagonal vs vertical based), estimating dynamical invariants (K2, D2, mutual information, point-wise dimension), handling noise and data-length requirements, and extending RPs to spatial data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding choice and its effect on RQA
rubrics_metrics.description: Although an embedding is not necessary for maps (i.e. m = 1), embedding (choice of embedding dimension m and delay τ) is often used; RQA measures typically depend rather strongly on the embedding parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use embedding when needed for comparison with other work; be aware that most RQA measures (e.g. DET, L, Lmax, LAM, TT, Vmax) are not invariant under different embeddings and can change significantly with m and τ. However, estimation of invariants K2 and D2 via the RP-based pc(ε,l) slope is independent of embedding (slope is preserved up to a shift, see relations p(m,τ)_c(ε,l) shifts). For scalar observations, embedding reconstruction remains necessary for many analyses, but check embedding-sensitivity when interpreting RQA statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold (ε) selection and recurrence rate trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: The cut-off distance ε determines which points are considered recurrent; in examples ε is chosen as 10% of the standard deviation (ε = 0.1σ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller ε distinguishes small variations better (useful near accumulation points) but reduces recurrence point density and worsens statistics of continuous structures in the RP. Choose ε mindful of the trade-off between resolution and sufficient recurrence density; one practical approach when comparing different systems is to choose thresholds that yield equal recurrence rates (RR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence point density considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The density of recurrence points influences statistical reliability of measured structures (diagonal/vertical lines) and derived measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid thresholds that lead to very sparse recurrence plots (poor statistics) or overly dense plots (loss of structure). When decreasing ε, expect fewer recurrence points and poorer statistics of continuous structures; adjust data length or ε to maintain adequate sample of lines for RQA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of RP line structures: diagonals vs vertical/horizontal
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagonal lines in an RP indicate co-moving trajectory segments (predictability / periodicity); vertical (and horizontal) lines indicate laminar behaviour (pauses, intermittency) and are prominent at chaos–chaos transitions such as band merging and inner crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visually, periodic states produce continuous, periodic diagonal lines but no vertical/horizontal lines. Chaos–chaos transitions produce vertically/horizontally spread black areas. Use the presence, length, and distribution of diagonal vs vertical structures to distinguish periodic, laminar/intermittent, and chaotic regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagonal-based RQA measures (DET, L, Lmax) and what they detect
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures based on diagonal lines (DET, L, Lmax) quantify predictability/regularity and show clear maxima at periodic–chaos / chaos–periodic transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lmax finds all periodic–chaos/chaos–periodic transitions in examples, while DET and L may miss some. These diagonal-based measures generally do not detect chaos–chaos transitions (e.g., inner crises, band merging). Use them primarily to identify transitions involving increased periodicity or predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical-based RQA measures (LAM, TT, Vmax) and what they detect
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures based on vertical structures (LAM, TT, Vmax) identify laminar states and chaos–chaos transitions; they show distinct maxima/peaks at such points and drop to zero within periodic windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LAM measures the amount (fraction) of laminar states, Vmax measures maximal duration of laminar states, and TT (trapping time) measures average vertical line length. LAM does not increase at inner crises in some examples (so differences between LAM and Vmax occur). Use vertical-based measures to detect intermittency, inner/outer crises, and band merging. Note: LAM is more robust against noise than TT and Vmax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noise sensitivity of RQA measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Noise affects detection of transitions: small noise levels still allow detection, but measures respond differently to noise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LAM is more robust against noise compared to TT and Vmax. Be cautious interpreting Vmax and TT peaks in noisy data; consider denoising, averaging, or focusing on more robust measures (LAM) when noise is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data length requirements for RQA vs other complexity measures
rubrics_metrics.description: RQA-based measures can work with much shorter time series (e.g. ~1,000 data points) whereas some formerly proposed complexity measures require much larger datasets (e.g. >100,000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For estimating K2 using RP methods, 10,000 points may suffice (Bernoulli example), but estimating D2 often requires many more points (Rössler D2 estimation used 200,000 points; stable estimation may need ≥50,000 depending on system complexity). Choose methods consistent with available data length and desired invariant (K2 easier than D2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating correlation entropy K2 from RP (pc(ε,l) slope)
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability pc(ε,l) to find a diagonal of at least length l in the RP scales as ~ε^{D2} e^{-l Δt K2}; an estimator is ˆK2(ε,l) = - (1/(l Δt)) ln(pc(ε,l)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot ln(pc(ε,l)) vs l for small ε and long lines: a linear region with slope = -ˆK2(ε) Δt yields K2. Use multiple ε to check consistency. This RP-based estimator links diagonal line-length distributions to correlation entropy, and is more directly related to K2 than to the maximal Lyapunov exponent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating correlation dimension D2 from RP
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the scaling pc(ε,l) ≈ ε^{D2} e^{-l Δt K2}, D2 can be estimated by comparing pc at two thresholds: ˆD2(ε) = ln(pc(ε,l)/pc(ε+Δε,l)) / ln(ε/(ε+Δε)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute pc for at least two nearby thresholds and use the logarithmic ratio to estimate D2. Average over appropriate l (e.g., lines in a scaling region). Be aware that D2 estimation is sensitive to choice of ε and scaling region; larger data sets are typically required for reliable D2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagonal line-length distribution relates to correlation entropy (not directly to Lyapunov)
rubrics_metrics.description: The distribution of diagonal lines is not directly related to the maximal Lyapunov exponent but to the correlation entropy K2; K2 is a lower bound for the sum of positive Lyapunov exponents (K2 ≤ Σ_{λ_i>0} λ_i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic heuristics that equate inverse average diagonal line length directly to the largest Lyapunov exponent. Use RP-based estimators for K2 and then relate K2 to Lyapunov exponents via formal inequalities if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple scaling regions and interpretation (recurrence period Trec)
rubrics_metrics.description: RPs can reveal multiple scaling regions in ln(pc(ε,l)) vs l (e.g., Rössler shows two regions); the first corresponds to short-term dynamics up to the recurrence period Trec, the second (long-l) slope yields K2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and separate scaling regions before estimating K2/D2. The transition point between slopes indicates Trec (recurrence period) and gives insight into characteristic time scales (Trec vs phase period Tph). For prediction tasks, slopes in different regions indicate different predictability regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding-invariance of RP-based K2 and D2 estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Although p(m,τ)_c(ε,l) shifts with embedding parameters, the slope of ln p(m,τ)_c(ε,l) used to estimate K2 is invariant under changes in embedding (up to shift of l); similarly, the D2 estimator via ratios is embedding-independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an advantage of RP methods over some other algorithms: when estimating K2 and D2 from diagonal line statistics, results should not depend on specific embedding choices (provided l large enough and relations l+(m−1)τ mapping respected). Use this property to reduce sensitivity to embedding when targeting invariants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence times (T^(1), T^(2)) and point-wise dimension DP(i)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define recurrence times from column recurrence points: T^(1)_k = j_k+1 - j_k (raw), but tangential motion causes spurious short recurrences; remove consecutive recurrences to compute Poincaré recurrence times T^(2). Mean recurrence times relate to the local measure µ(B_xi(ε)) ≈ 1 / mean recurrence time, and scaling µ(B_xi(ε)) ∼ ε^{DP(i)} gives point-wise dimension DP(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate recurrence times either from recurrence index sets or average lengths of white vertical lines. Be cautious: tangential motion biases T^(1); using T^(2) (removing tangential neighbors) or averaging white vertical lines can mitigate bias. For scalar time series with embedding, T^(2) is more robust for non-stationarity analysis. Use sliding windows over time to monitor changes in mean recurrence times for transient detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual information and cross mutual information estimation via RPs
rubrics_metrics.description: The second-order Rényi entropy H2 and joint entropy H2(τ) can be estimated from recurrence/count matrices, enabling estimation of generalized mutual information I2(τ) and cross mutual information between components/systems using (joint) recurrence matrices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formulas ˆH2 = -ln( (1/N^2) Σ_{i,j} R_{i,j} ) and ˆH2(τ) with delayed/joint recurrence matrices; ˆI2 = ˆH2 + ˆH2(y) - ˆH2(x,y) or the given recurrence-based equivalents. When comparing systems with different phase-space scales, choose thresholds so recurrence rates are equal (RR) to equilibrate phase-space size differences; then ˜I2 = ln( (1/N^2) Σ JR_{i,j} ) - 2 ln RR. Note: choice of norm (maximum vs Euclidean) affects estimates—using maximum norm can make RP-based and correlation-sum-based mutual information agree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold choice for comparing different systems (match recurrence rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: When estimating cross mutual information or comparing RQA across systems with different phase-space diameters, thresholds ε_x and ε_y should be equilibrated, e.g., by choosing them so that both systems have the same recurrence rate RR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute recurrence rates 1/N^2 Σ R_x = 1/N^2 Σ R_y = RR, then use joint recurrence counts and subtract 2 ln RR to form a balanced mutual information estimate. This reduces bias due to differences in scale between systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of norm affects RP-derived invariants and mutual information
rubrics_metrics.description: Using different norms (maximum norm vs Euclidean) changes recurrence counts and therefore estimated quantities; in examples, maximum norm makes RP-based mutual information coincide with correlation-sum approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the norm used and, if comparing methods or reproducing results, use the same norm (maximum norm recommended when comparing to correlation-sum-based estimates). Consider testing sensitivity to norm choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of RPs to spatial (high-dimensional) data
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurrence concept extends to spatial data by defining spatial recurrence plots: R_{ĩ,ĵ} = Θ(ε - ||x_{ĩ} - x_{ĵ}||), where indices are d-dimensional coordinates; the resulting RP has dimension 2d and contains diagonal-oriented hyper-surfaces (hyper-surface of identity HSOI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define diagonal hyper-surfaces and vertical hyper-surfaces in the spatial RP analogous to diagonal/vertical lines in temporal RPs. Compute frequency distributions of hyper-surface sizes and apply recurrence quantification measures to these distributions to characterize spatial data (images, snapshots). For 2D images with scalar values, the RP is 4D and HSOI is 2D—quantification must operate on hyper-surfaces rather than simple lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical example parameter recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Worked examples use embedding m = 3, τ = 1 and threshold ε = 0.1σ for logistic-map studies; other worked examples used thresholds and data lengths appropriate to the system (e.g., 10,000 points for Bernoulli K2 estimates, 200,000 for Rössler D2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these example settings as starting points, but adjust for system complexity and data availability: shorter chaotic maps may be analyzed without embedding (m=1), while higher-dimensional continuous systems require larger data sets and careful threshold/embedding choices.
